newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Eight killed in tribal feud in Nigerian oil area.
newsitem.headline: Eight killed in tribal feud in Nigerian oil area.

text.p: Eight people were killed on Monday in the troubled Nigerian oil city of Warri in running clashes between youths of rival tribes, residents said.
"Armed youths barricaded roads linking Ekurede and Okere areas of Warri before unleashing terror this afternoon," said a journalist from Warri, 300 kms (190 miles) east of Lagos.
He said the latest casualties were from the Ijaw and Itsekiri tribes, which have been at loggerheads since the government moved local council headquarters from an Ijaw to an Itsekiri town.
Monday's killings bring to 58 the number of lives lost in renewed fighting since April 12 around Warri, where unrest first broke out on March 22.
Oil industry sources said on Monday the renewed clashes could affect the operations of the sector that economically sustains Africa's most populous nation.

The local unit of oil giant Royal Dutch Shell Group, the biggest oil operator in the country, said the crisis had so far shut one flow station and its output was running 2,000 barrels per day (bpd) below normal.
The Nigerian unit of Chevron Corp said its operation had not been affected.
But industry sources said oil services firms which supply materials to the major companies were concerned.
"The worry in the oil industry is palpable," said one senior oil company executive," adding: "It is common knowledge that gangs of youths have lots of arms about in the area."
Armed youths on Saturday attacked an oil services company boat on the high seas and kidnapped its Nigerian captain.
The boat, belonging to the Nigerian-owned Sea Truck Nigeria Limited, was carrying exploration equipment and supplies to oil installations in nearby Forcados.
The military government immediately deployed a fast attack navy ship, the NNS Ekpe, to the area, saying its objective was to ensure oil production was not affected.
A dusk-to-dawn curfew imposed in Warri after the March clashes was lifted last week.

At the height of the March crisis, armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six Shell oil flow stations, shutting a total of 100,000 bpd there. A total of 127 of Shell's Nigerian staff held hostage by the tribesmen were released in batches following delicate negotiations and oil output has since resumed.
At the root of the crisis in Warri area is a rivalry among three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and the Urhobos.
The Urhobos controlled affairs there in the 1970s until the Itsekiris, who provide the paramount ruler for Warri, began to press for more say in the town in the 1980s.
The Ijaws, who inhabit the riverine areas and have a bigger population also began asking for more amenities in their areas.
